approachQuestion.prompt:
Lighting adjustments. There are n initially zero brightness values. Each of m commands (left, right, delta) adds delta to every position in the inclusive range. All commands are provided before any result is needed. Return the final n values.

Input: n=5, commands [(1,3,4), (0,1,-2), (3,4,1)]. Output: [-2,2,4,5,1].

Constraints: 1 ≤ n,m ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ left ≤ right < n. -1000000 ≤ delta ≤ 1000000. Values may be negative. Commands are read-only. There are no intermediate queries or clipping of values. All arithmetic fits signed 64-bit integers.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Allocate a zero array D of n+1 entries. For each command add delta at D[left] and subtract delta at D[right+1]. Scan indices 0 through n-1 with a running total and write that total to the result.
options.feedback: The start event activates the adjustment and the event after the right endpoint cancels it. Summing events combines overlapping commands.

options.text: Initialize the result to zero; for every command, add delta individually to each covered position.
options.feedback: This is correct, but many full-length commands repeatedly traverse the same positions. Recording just their boundaries avoids that work.

options.text: Record delta at left and -delta at right, then accumulate the event array.
options.feedback: It cancels too early. For n=1 and command (0,0,7), the result becomes 0 instead of 7.

options.text: Set D[left]=delta and D[right+1]=-delta for each command, then accumulate D.
options.feedback: Shared boundaries must combine additions. Two commands (0,0,2) on n=1 should produce 4; overwriting produces 2.

feedback.reason: Record each addition at its first affected position and its cancellation just after the last affected position. Combine events by addition, then scan once with a running total to recover each final brightness.
details: Record each addition at its first affected position and its cancellation just after the last affected position. Combine events by addition, then scan once with a running total to recover each final brightness.

An inclusive addition begins at left and stops immediately after right. The cancellation belongs at right+1, not right. Overlapping commands add their events before the cumulative scan reconstructs final brightness.

“Allocate a zero array D of n+1 entries. For each command add delta at D[left] and subtract delta at D[right+1]. Scan indices 0 through n-1 with a running total and write that total to the result.”: The start event activates the adjustment and the event after the right endpoint cancels it. Summing events combines overlapping commands.

“Initialize the result to zero; for every command, add delta individually to each covered position.”: This is correct, but many full-length commands repeatedly traverse the same positions. Recording just their boundaries avoids that work.
“Record delta at left and -delta at right, then accumulate the event array.”: It cancels too early. For n=1 and command (0,0,7), the result becomes 0 instead of 7.
“Set D[left]=delta and D[right+1]=-delta for each command, then accumulate D.”: Shared boundaries must combine additions. Two commands (0,0,2) on n=1 should produce 4; overwriting produces 2.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest worst-case time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Analyze the explicitly allocated D array, separate from the required result. Exclude input commands and result storage. Arithmetic and array access are constant time.

options.text: O(n + m) time; O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + m) time; O(1) auxiliary space
O(n log n + m) time; O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Two events per command replace repeated visits to every affected slot.
details: Initialize n+1 events, record two events per command, then scan n positions.
Analyze the explicitly allocated D array, separate from the required result. Exclude input commands and result storage. Arithmetic and array access are constant time.
D holds n+1 signed values. Running total and loop indices are constant space; no recursion or input copying. An implementation that reuses output storage is a different method.
Direct updates use O(nm) time and no additional array beyond output; the two incorrect event methods fail even on single-position ranges.
